basic_identification.name: No shared knowledge graph for the field
basic_identification.originator: Structural absence — no single organization or community has attempted to build a Getty-equivalent for digital art. The closest efforts (Wikidata art properties, Rhizome ArtBase metadata, Feral File artist bios) are siloed and incomplete.
basic_identification.year: Ongoing since ~2015; became acute post-2021 NFT boom when field scale outpaced vocabulary
basic_identification.key_url: No primary URL — this is a gap, not an entity. Reference points: Getty ULAN (https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/ulan/), Getty AAT (https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/aat/), Wikidata (https://www.wikidata.org/)
basic_identification.geography: Global — the absence is universal across all digital art communities

core_ideas.core_claim: The digital art field lacks a structured, shared vocabulary or relational map equivalent to what traditional art has in Getty ULAN (Union List of Artist Names), AAT (Art & Architecture Thesaurus), or ICONCLASS. Without this, the field cannot systematically name its practitioners, movements, concepts, or relationships.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Digital art's rapid evolution, hybrid practices (code + visual + performance + AI), platform fragmentation, and pseudonymous culture make traditional art classification systems inadequate. The field needs a vocabulary that can handle generative processes, on-chain provenance, algorithmic authorship, and cross-platform identities — none of which traditional art ontologies were designed for.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: The absence of a knowledge graph means the field's legibility is entirely mediated by platform algorithms. Without structured relational data, discovery defaults to engagement metrics (likes, sales volume, follower counts). Artists and works that don't perform well algorithmically become structurally invisible regardless of their significance. The knowledge graph gap directly enables the attention economy's dominance over the field's self-understanding.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: This gap is purely an infrastructure absence — it is neither attention-native nor intention-native. However, filling it would be a fundamentally intention-native act: creating shared vocabulary serves the field's declared structural needs rather than capturing engagement. The gap's persistence reflects the field's under-investment in intention-driven infrastructure.

market_economics.revenue_model: None — a gap has no revenue model. Building the infrastructure to fill it would likely require grants, institutional funding, or commons-based funding (potentially DAO or protocol funding). Getty vocabularies are sustained by the Getty Trust endowment.
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure (absent). Would sit at the foundation layer of the value chain, enabling all other market functions (discovery, valuation, curation, preservation) to operate with shared reference points.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: The gap is widening. The field has grown significantly (AI art, generative art, on-chain art) but vocabulary and relational infrastructure have not kept pace. Post-crash, some consolidation has occurred but no systematic knowledge structuring has emerged.
market_economics.collector_demographics: Not applicable — this is a gap, not a market entity
market_economics.sustainability: The absence itself is self-sustaining because no single actor has sufficient incentive to build commons infrastructure. Platform companies benefit from proprietary data silos. Individual artists lack resources. Institutions (museums, universities) have been slow to engage with digital art's specificity. Filling this gap requires a commons-oriented actor willing to invest without immediate return — exactly the kind of entity that market logic does not produce.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Existing partial tools: Wikidata (open linked data), Schema.org (web-standard metadata), Dublin Core (library metadata), IPFS (content addressing for permanence). No tool currently synthesizes these for digital art specifically.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: AI could be a powerful tool for building the knowledge graph (entity extraction, relationship mapping, taxonomy generation from unstructured text). However, AI-generated ontologies risk encoding biases and flattening contested categories. The knowledge graph should be AI-assisted but human-governed. AI training datasets would also benefit enormously from a structured knowledge graph of the field.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: This is precisely the problem. The aesthetic vocabulary for digital art is fragmented, informal, platform-specific, and often borrowed from adjacent fields (computer science, traditional art, crypto culture). Terms like 'generative,' 'on-chain,' 'long-form,' 'PFP,' 'AI art' carry contested meanings. No authority or shared reference can disambiguate. Critical discourse lacks stable referents.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Filling this gap would position strongly toward: openness (shared vocabulary must be open), commons (knowledge as public infrastructure), infrastructure (foundational layer, not spectacle), collective (field-level resource, not individual). The gap itself represents the absence of these values in practice.

infrastructure_governance.openness: The gap exists partly because existing vocabularies are either proprietary (platform-specific taxonomies on SuperRare, Art Blocks, Foundation) or not adapted for digital art (Getty vocabularies are open but traditional-art-focused). Filling it requires open, CC-licensed, machine-readable data.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: None — the gap has no governance. Building the knowledge graph would require deciding on governance: expert-committee (like Getty), community-driven (like Wikidata), DAO-based, or hybrid. This governance question is itself a design challenge.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Currently, relational data about digital artists is scattered across platforms that own and control it. Artists cannot export their relational context (who they've collaborated with, which movements they belong to, how their work relates to others). Each platform holds fragments.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Zero interoperability — the fragments that exist (platform artist profiles, marketplace metadata, social media bios) use incompatible schemas. No shared identifiers, no linked data, no API standards for digital art metadata.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: No preservation strategy exists for the field's relational knowledge. Individual works may be preserved (IPFS, on-chain), but the relationships between them — influence, movement membership, conceptual lineage — are preserved only in ephemeral social media posts and articles.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Absent. No mechanism exists for artists to consent to or contest their classification, categorization, or relational positioning within any knowledge structure.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Traditional art has solved this problem (Getty ULAN has 304,000+ artist records, AAT has 70,000+ concepts). Digital art's failure to build equivalent infrastructure widens the gap between traditional and digital art worlds, making institutional integration harder.
field_position.what_it_enables: Nothing — this is an absence. Filling it would enable: systematic discovery beyond algorithms, contextual understanding of artists' work, curriculum development for education, curatorial research, market analysis with shared reference points, historical documentation, and cross-platform identity resolution.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Everything. There is no shared vocabulary, no relational map, no classification system, no authority file, no linked data infrastructure for the digital art field.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Everyone suffers from this gap, but especially: artists working outside major platforms, practitioners in non-English-speaking communities, those working across categories that platforms don't recognize, historical digital artists whose work predates current platforms, and researchers/curators trying to map the field.
field_position.frontier_signal: Emerging awareness. Several projects gesture toward this (Artacle, various blockchain analytics tools, museum digitization efforts) but none have attempted a comprehensive field-level knowledge graph. The need is increasingly recognized in discourse around digital art infrastructure.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Currently: none (this is the gap). Discovery in the field defaults to social media algorithms, marketplace trending pages, and word of mouth — all attention-economy mechanisms.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: The absence of a knowledge graph makes the entire field maximally dependent on attention-economy platforms for legibility. If a structured knowledge graph existed, the field could be navigated independently of any single platform.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Building this infrastructure would be the most intention-native intervention possible: creating shared, open, structural vocabulary that serves the field's declared needs rather than any platform's engagement metrics.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: The gap represents the total absence of commons-level knowledge infrastructure. Every entity in the field currently encloses its own fragment of relational data. No commons contribution exists.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Neither — the gap means no provenance of meaning (conceptual lineage, influence, movement membership) is systematically tracked. On-chain provenance tracks ownership but not meaning.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: None — without a knowledge graph, the field has no systematic temporal record of how concepts, movements, and relationships have evolved.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: This item IS the absence. It represents the most fundamental missing infrastructure in the digital art field — the inability to name and relate its own constituents.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Neither — the gap prevents both. Without shared vocabulary, the field cannot achieve even coherence (multiple valid readings coexisting within a shared frame). Disagreements cannot be productive because there are no stable referents to disagree about.
coherence.contestability: No contestability mechanism exists because there is nothing structured to contest. Informal disagreements about categorization happen on social media but leave no structured trace.
coherence.forkability: Not applicable — cannot fork what does not exist. However, any future knowledge graph should be designed for forkability from the start.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: A(DAI) should treat this gap as its founding rationale. The project should study Getty ULAN/AAT architecture (linked data, authority files, hierarchical relationships, scope notes) and adapt these patterns for digital art's specific needs (pseudonymous identities, algorithmic authorship, cross-platform presence, on-chain provenance). Wikidata's community governance model and open-data principles are also instructive.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: A(DAI) must refuse: (1) the illusion that a single authoritative taxonomy can capture the field — coherence without consensus means multiple valid categorizations must coexist; (2) any approach that requires complete data before being useful — the graph must be useful at every stage of incompleteness; (3) any governance model that concentrates naming power in a small group without contestability.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: The tension is between comprehensiveness and humility. A knowledge graph implies authority (who decides what counts, what relates to what), but A(DAI)'s architecture demands contestability and coherence-without-consensus. Building infrastructure that structures without over-determining is the core design challenge.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: A knowledge graph containing artist information would be subject to GDPR/privacy regulations (personal data of artists, especially those using real names). Pseudonymous artists raise questions about right to be forgotten vs. historical record. No direct AI Act exposure unless AI is used in classification. [uncertain]
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Any knowledge graph filling this gap should be CC0 or CC-BY for maximum reuse. Getty vocabularies use Open Data Commons Attribution License. Wikidata uses CC0.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Critical design question. Should artists be included by default (opt-out) like Wikipedia, or only with explicit consent (opt-in)? Opt-in limits coverage; opt-out raises consent concerns. A(DAI)'s consent architecture must address this directly.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: The gap exists because the field is dependent on platforms that enclose relational data. Building the knowledge graph would reduce platform dependency field-wide.
ecosystem.network_effects: A knowledge graph would be the ultimate network-effect infrastructure — each new node (artist, concept, work, movement) increases the value of all existing nodes through new connections. Currently, these network effects are captured by platforms (SuperRare, Art Blocks, Foundation) rather than shared as commons.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: The gap has become more visible post-crash. During the 2021-2022 boom, the absence was masked by volume and hype. Post-crash, the field's inability to articulate its own structure, history, and value beyond speculative metrics has become painfully apparent. Growing recognition that infrastructure is needed.
